paras: The lynching of William Hopkins took place on the night of May 21, 1903, at White's Mill, Georgia, where a mob shot to death a Black man who was being taken to jail by train. Hopkins had been charged with outraging his nine-year-old stepdaughter at Babcock in Miller County. An Associated Press dispatch from Bainbridge carried the news to papers from Georgia to Maine and Minnesota, several of which headlined the charge against him rather than the killing.

According to the dispatch, Hopkins was charged with outraging his nine-year-old stepdaughter at Babcock, a place the Savannah Morning News printed as "Dabcock." The Daily Kennebec Journal of Augusta, Maine, described the charge as "assaulting" the girl and printed his name once as "Wm. Popkins" before calling him Hopkins. The same dispatch stated that "the negro confessed the crime," without saying to whom or under what circumstances.

On the night of Thursday, May 21, Hopkins was being conveyed to jail on a Georgia, Florida and Alabama train. Most versions say he was in the charge of a single officer, while the Dawson News, a Georgia weekly, said he was taken from "officers." A mob removed him from the train and shot him to death at White's Mill. The coverage names neither the officer nor any member of the mob, and it does not report how many men took part.
No report of an inquest, arrest or grand-jury inquiry appears in the coverage, which ends with weekly news digests at the close of May.

The story reached the white press as a single Associated Press dispatch dated Bainbridge, May 22, which ran on May 23 in the Savannah Morning News, the Raleigh News & Observer, the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Indianapolis Journal, the Wheeling Register and two Maine dailies. The Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger followed on May 26 and the Dawson News on May 27, while weeklies in North Dakota and Minnesota reduced it to a single sentence in their news digests.

Headlines framed the killing in different ways. The Savannah Morning News headed it "Lynched a Negro. His Revolting Crime Had Infuriated the Mob," and the Wilmington paper called it "Brute Lynched in Georgia." The Raleigh News & Observer ran it as "Outraged His Stepchild. This is Why William Hopkins Dies of an Overdose of Lead." In Maine, the Portland Daily Press placed it beside an Indiana assault case under "The Negro Problem. A Lynching and a Case That Seems To Call For Another." Closer to the scene, the Dawson News used the headline "Mob Law in Miller," though it repeated the confession claim, and other papers used plain headings such as "Negro Shot By Mob."

Every account presented the charge against Hopkins and his reported confession as fact, and none carried a statement from his family or any Black witness. No coverage of the lynching was found in the Black press.
Apart from the spelling of his name and the number of officers, the versions agree, since all derive from the same dispatch.

reader.title: Lynching of William Hopkins
bases: A mob took a Black prisoner charged with a crime from an officer on a train and shot him to death (A1, A10).

Hopkins was shot to death by a 'mob' after being taken from an officer conveying him to jail on a charge of outraging his stepdaughter (A1, A4, A10); the killing was punishment outside the law for an alleged crime.

Every report found is a version of one Associated Press dispatch dated Bainbridge, May 22 (A1, A2, A4), including the Georgia weekly's rewrite (A10); no independent local report, inquest or follow-up was found.

The Indianapolis Journal, Birmingham Age-Herald and Wheeling Register ran the dispatch under plain headlines such as 'Negro Shot By Mob'.

conflicts.note: 'Popkins' appears once in one condensed item that itself switches to 'Hopkins'; it is a misprint.
The Georgia weekly's plural is the only variant; the dispatch it reworked says one officer.
'Dabcock' is a typographic or OCR error in one paper.
